extracted.intended_audience: Voters and citizens of the State of New York; readers engaged in the constitutional debate about the structure and powers of the national Executive
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria and arguments for designing and assessing the national Executive in a constitution, discussing what makes an Executive 'energetic' and 'safe' and comparing presidential powers with those of monarchs and state governors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Veto power (qualified negative)
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is to have power to return a bill, which shall have passed the two branches of the legislature, for reconsideration; and the bill so returned is to become a law, if, upon that reconsideration, it be approved by two thirds of both houses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with the British king's absolute negative on acts of Parliament; the President's veto is a qualified, revisory power requiring a supermajority override. The passage notes the political reality that absolute negatives may be avoided by influence and majorities, and emphasizes the difference in institutional form and effect between a qualified veto and an absolute royal negative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commander-in-chief authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is to be the 'commander-in-chief of the army and navy of the United States, and of the militia of the several States, when called into the actual service of the United States.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scope is limited: (1) militia command only when called into actual national service (not perpetual control), (2) president's military authority does not include declaring war or raising/regulating fleets and armies (those are legislative powers). Comparisons with the British monarch and some state governors show the president's role is more nominal/supreme-in-command but substantively narrower.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pardoning power (limited)
rubrics_metrics.description: He is to have power to grant reprieves and pardons for offenses against the United States, except in cases of impeachment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast to some state governors (e.g., governor of New York) who may pardon in a broader set of cases (the text notes the governor of New York may pardon even in cases of impeachment, except for treason and murder). The paper discusses political consequences of broad pardoning (e.g., sheltering conspirators prior to treason) and argues the constitutional limitation reduces temptation to misuse the power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommend measures and legislative convening/adjournment powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The President may recommend to the consideration of Congress such measures as he shall judge necessary and expedient; to convene, on extraordinary occasions, both houses, or either of them; and, in case of disagreement between them with respect to the time of adjournment, to adjourn them to such time as he shall think proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are executive tools to influence legislation and handle extraordinary circumstances; they enable initiative and maintenance of governance continuity without constant legislative sessions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treaty-making with Senate consent
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is to have power, with the advice and consent of the Senate, to make treaties, provided two thirds of the senators present concur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a concurrent national prerogative requiring legislative concurrence; contrasted with the British king's sole treaty-making power. The text emphasizes that requiring Senate concurrence both limits unilateral executive foreign power and concentrates treaty prerogative at the federal (not state) level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Receiving ambassadors (dignitary role)
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is also to be authorized to receive ambassadors and other public ministers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterized as more a matter of dignity than substantive authority; arranged for convenience so the legislature need not be convened on every arrival of a foreign minister.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointments: nomination with Senate advice and consent
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is to nominate, and, with the advice and consent of the Senate, to appoint ambassadors and other public ministers, judges of the Supreme Court, and in general all officers of the United States established by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compared to the British king (who appoints and creates offices) and state practices (e.g., New York's governor plus council), the federal appointment process is more public and requires larger bodies' concurrence. Practical effects noted: publicity and a larger confirming body reduce ease of influence, while small state councils are easier to sway and may allow executive dominance via casting votes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ingredients constituting energy in the Executive
rubrics_metrics.description: The ingredients which constitute energy in the Executive are, first, unity; secondly, duration; thirdly, an adequate provision for its support; fourthly, competent powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four features are presented as necessary components for an effective (energetic) executive: a single, decisive authority (unity); sufficient tenure (duration) to act independently; adequate material support to perform duties; and powers commensurate with responsibilities. The essay discusses trade-offs in combining energy with republican safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ingredients constituting safety in a republic
rubrics_metrics.description: The ingredients which constitute safety in the republican sense are, first, a due dependence on the people, secondly, a due responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Safety requires that the executive be answerable to popular will and subject to mechanisms of responsibility (censure, removal, punishment). These must be balanced against energy—design should combine energetic authority with dependence and accountability to prevent abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of the Executive (advantages and threats to unity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity is conducive to energy: decision, activity, secrecy, and despatch will generally characterize the proceedings of one man in a much more eminent degree than the proceedings of any greater number; this unity may be destroyed by vesting the power in two or more magistrates of equal dignity and authority or by vesting it ostensibly in one man subject to the control and co-operation of others (councils).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments given: plurality produces dissension, weakens authority, impedes critical measures (especially in war), conceals faults, and destroys responsibility. Examples: Roman consuls, state executive councils. Unity creates a single object for popular jealousy and scrutiny, making confinement of executive power easier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plurality/council disadvantages: concealment of faults and dilution of responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The multiplication of the Executive adds to the difficulty of detection [of misconduct]... Responsibility is of two kinds—to censure and to punishment. The multiplication of the Executive adds to the difficulty of detection in either case. It often becomes impossible, amidst mutual accusations, to determine on whom the blame... ought really to fall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plural executives enable mutual blame-shifting, ambiguity about authorship of bad measures, and reduced efficacy of public censure and punishment; councils can be used as pretexts ('I was overruled by my council'), reducing accountability. In monarchies councils can substitute for the monarch's lack of responsibility, but in republics they undermine intended personal responsibility of the chief magistrate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration in office promotes firmness and stability
rubrics_metrics.description: The longer the duration in office, the greater will be the probability of obtaining personal firmness of the executive in the employment of his constitutional powers and the stability of the system of administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short or uncertain tenure incentivizes servility and feebleness—an executive seeking re-election or holding office briefly will be less willing to encounter public or legislative ill-humors. Longer tenure fosters independence from transient popular passions and aids continuity of administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-offs of council size and separation of powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Numbers in an executive council must be so great as to render combination difficult, or they are rather a source of danger than of security... The united credit and influence of several individuals must be more formidable to liberty than the credit and influence of either of them separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small councils are vulnerable to collusion and influence; large councils are costly and unwieldy. A council to a responsible magistrate often acts as a clog on good intentions, an accomplice in bad ones, and a cloak for faults. Practical considerations include expense, ease of influencing few members, and loss of clear public accountability.
